## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Matthew Henry says the disciples' old quarrels about who was greatest had ended, and they had been praying together. Anyone wanting the Spirit poured out should first be "of one accord." [MHC] A sermon quoted in the Precept Austin PDF says revival can't come where Christians are fighting, and points to Acts 1:14. [PApdf] Another older commentator says they waited and prayed patiently, probably gathered in the upper room, and that people who want the Spirit's power still need to wait expectantly in prayer. [BH4] Guzik says you must recognise your emptiness before you can be filled. By gathering to pray in obedience, the disciples admitted they couldn't do the work in their own strength. [EW]

**v. 2:** Boice, quoted by Precept Austin, links the wind to the Spirit over the waters at creation (Gen 1), God breathing life into Adam (Gen 2:7) and "born again" (John 3). He sees Pentecost as a new creation. [PA]

**v. 3:** Guzik says fire usually pictures purifying, so the Spirit's filling is about purity, not just power. He also says we shouldn't expect wind or flames today, though we can receive the same filling. [EW] The Precept Austin PDF calls fire an emblem of the Spirit because it spreads, consumes and warms. [PApdf] Calvin says God could have equipped the apostles without any signs, but the signs were given to help every later age. [CAL]

**v. 4:**
- **Gill:** The disciples already had the Spirit as a Spirit of grace. Now they were filled to overflowing with his gifts, and this was the baptism with the Spirit promised in Acts 1:5. They spoke real languages they had never learned (the "new tongues" of Mark 16:17), and sometimes one person spoke several. What they said was orderly, weighty and understood: "the wonderful works of God." [SL]
- **Another older commentator:** The miracle was in the speakers' mouths, not the hearers' ears. Each disciple could speak different languages as needed, fluently, as if native. The scene is set against Babel. [BH4]
- **Another older commentator:** All 120 were filled, not just the apostles, which shows "all Christians have the Spirit." The heart of Pentecost was the giving of the Spirit, not the sound, fire or tongues. A Spirit-filled person naturally speaks about Christ. [BH4]
- **Calvin:** The apostles were given real languages so they could truly communicate with their hearers. He leaves it open whether there was also a second miracle in the hearing. [CAL]
- **Matthew Henry:** They received miraculous powers to spread the gospel, and spoke "as the Spirit gave them utterance," not from planning beforehand. [MHC]
- **Guzik:** The flames resting on each person mark a shift. In the Old Testament the Spirit rested on Israel as a nation; in the New Covenant he lives in each believer. He lists earlier stages in the disciples' experience of the Spirit, including John 20:19–23, and says groups as well as individuals can be filled. [EW]

**vv. 5–11:** Ellicott says the word "proselytes" here probably means its strictest sense: full converts received into Israel's covenant ("proselytes of righteousness"). [ELL] Precept Austin says these were real foreign languages. At Babel God split people up by confusing their languages; at Pentecost he broke down national barriers. [PA] Another older commentator says the "wonderful works of God" were probably the story of the crucified and ascended Jesus. [BH4] Ellicott's reading is that the disciples, who used to worship apart from foreign pilgrims, could now share fellowship with worshippers from every land. [BH4][SL]

**vv. 12–13:** Precept Austin says everything in vv. 1–13 prepared the crowd to hear Peter's answer to "What does this mean?" [PA] Guzik says the tongues produced only amazement and mockery. Conviction came only when the gospel was preached. [EW] Ellicott says the word for "new wine" implies fermentation, and the jibe suggests the disciples' tone and manner looked excited. [ELL]

**v. 14:** Guzik says Peter spoke for the whole group of apostles, the tongues stopped when he began to preach, and his boldness was a striking change from his earlier denials. [EW][EW-dev1] He also says Luke gives an inspired summary of a longer sermon (see v. 40). [EW-dev1] Ellicott notes that the verb for "addressed" is the same unusual word as "utterance" in v. 4. That signals Peter's sermon was just as much a Spirit-given utterance as the tongues. [ELL]

**v. 15:** Barnes, quoted by Precept Austin, says Peter answered calmly and respectfully but firmly. Barnes takes this as a model for answering mockers, following 1 Peter 3:15. [PA2]

**v. 16:** Precept Austin says the phrase "through the prophet" pictures the prophets as channels through whom God spoke. [PA]

**v. 17:** MacArthur, quoted by Precept Austin, says "last days" was a name for the time of the Messiah. So Peter's claim that those days had begun would have shocked his hearers. [PA2] Steven Cole says Joel doesn't mention tongues. Peter's point is that the Spirit is poured out "on all flesh," not just on prophets or rabbis. [PA2] Guzik says the Spirit was once given in drops and is now poured out. [EW]

**v. 18:** Ellicott says the gift now goes even to male and female slaves, not only priests or trained prophets, because God shows no favouritism. He gives Amos the herdsman as an early example. [ELL] Another older commentator calls this "the true democracy of Christianity." [BH4]

**vv. 19–20:** Guzik lists these signs only as part of Joel's prophecy about the Day of the Lord. [EW-dev2] Nothing else was found.

**v. 21:** Guzik says Peter used the verse evangelistically: salvation is now offered to anyone who calls on the Lord, Jew or Gentile. [EW]

**v. 22:** Guzik says Joel and the Spirit's work were important, but the sermon wasn't complete until Peter preached Jesus. This verse is Peter's "second introduction." [EW-dev2] Precept Austin says "attested" means "proven" and is in the perfect tense (a past action with lasting effect). The words "to you" suggest some listeners had seen the miracles themselves. A. T. Robertson agrees. [PA]

**v. 23:** Precept Austin says "by the hands of" means "by means of," and the lawless men are the pagan Romans, including Pilate by implication (Acts 4:27). [PA] MacArthur says God used evil men to carry out his purpose without overriding their will or removing their guilt, so total sovereignty and full human responsibility stand side by side (compare Luke 22:22). Steven Cole says no one can blame God for their own sin. [PA][PA2]

**v. 24:** Precept Austin says God raising Jesus shows the Father accepted the Son's sacrifice. Because Jesus stayed God's Holy One through the cross, death couldn't hold him, and the resurrection proves his payment for sin was complete. [PA] Guzik says the same: because God's Holy One couldn't be held by death, the resurrection was "absolutely inevitable." [EW]

## 2. Where readings differ (only what these pages show)

**v. 3, did the flames stay?** Guzik says the word "sat" suggests permanence and settled purpose. [EW] Ellicott says the verb tense means a momentary action: the flames landed briefly and vanished. [ELL]

**v. 4, what were the tongues?**
- Gill, Calvin and another older commentator say they were real, unlearned human languages. [SL][CAL][BH4]
- Ellicott (Anglican) reads Pentecost alongside 1 Corinthians 14. There, he concludes, tongues were "the ecstatic utterance of rapturous devotion" rather than languages. He also allows the language reading as "the more natural" one for Acts 2. He calls the disciples' state "rapturous ecstasy." [SL][BH4]
- **Do tongues continue?** Ellicott sees no evidence the language power lasted beyond these outpourings. [BH4] Guzik encourages believers to seek the Spirit's filling today, but for bold witness rather than displays. [EW]

**vv. 13–15, did they look drunk?** Guzik says "being drunk in the Spirit" has no basis in Scripture, and quotes Stott that the fruit of the Spirit is self-control. [EW] Ellicott thinks the mockery suggests the disciples really did seem excited in tone and manner. [ELL]

**vv. 16–21, how was Joel fulfilled?**
- Guzik: Pentecost was a "near" fulfilment, with the final fulfilment still to come. [EW]
- Precept Austin, following MacArthur: a partial fulfilment. [PA]
- William MacDonald (quoted by Precept Austin): the prophecy has two fulfilments. The Spirit wasn't literally poured on all flesh at Pentecost, and the full fulfilment comes at the end of the Tribulation (an end-times reading). [PA]
- Precept Austin also says the church began at Pentecost, though its author says he is "not a dispensationalist." [PApdf]

**v. 23:** The pages present this as sovereignty plus human responsibility (MacArthur, Cole). [PA] I couldn't find a Methodist or Lutheran response.

**Spirit-baptism and later fillings:** Gill identifies this filling with the Spirit-baptism of Acts 1:5 and notes the disciples already had the Spirit before it. [SL] Guzik describes stages in their experience of the Spirit and repeated fillings (4:31). [EW] I couldn't reach any Pentecostal-denominational (ag.org), Wesleyan or Lutheran pages to compare.
